chapter: Ch 10: Accounting Standards for Consolidated Financial Statements
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Concept of Group, Holding Company, and Subsidiary Company
explain: A holding company is an enterprise that controls one or more other companies.
A subsidiary company is an entity controlled by a parent holding company.
Control is established by owning more than one-half of voting power.
Control also exists by controlling the composition of the Board of Directors.
Together, a parent company and all its subsidiaries form a group.
Legally they are distinct units, but economically they operate as a single body.

flow.title: Establishing Parent-Subsidiary Relationship
steps: Evaluate ownership of voting power
Check if voting rights exceed 50%
Alternatively verify Board composition control
Confirm parent holds power to appoint/remove directors
Parent and subsidiary form a Group

topics.example: Reliance Industries Limited controls Jio Platforms Limited by holding majority voting power, making them a group.
remember: Holding company is under Section 2(46) and Subsidiary company is under Section 2(87).
Control means more than 50% voting power or Board control.
mistakes: Assuming exactly 50% voting power gives control; the law requires more than one-half.

quiz.q: Which section of the Companies Act, 2013 defines a subsidiary company?
quiz.why: Section 2(87) defines a subsidiary company, while Section 2(46) defines a holding company.

quiz.q: Control over the Board of Directors means the power to appoint or remove:
o: All or a majority of directors
quiz.why: Control exists when an enterprise can appoint or remove all or a majority of the directors.

topics.title: Statutory Framework and Restrictions on Subsidiary Shareholding
explain: Section 19 prohibits a subsidiary from holding shares in its parent company.
Any allotment or transfer of parent shares to its subsidiary is void.
Exceptions apply if held as legal representative or trustee of another.
A subsidiary may also continue holding shares owned prior to becoming a subsidiary.
Voting rights are restricted only to shares held as legal representative or trustee.
Section 129 mandates presenting consolidated accounts along with standalone accounts at the AGM.

flow.title: Assessing Subsidiary Shareholding in Holding Company
steps: Subsidiary acquires shares in holding company
Check if holding is under statutory exceptions
If held as representative, trustee, or past holder: valid
If no valid exception: allotment is void
Restrict voting power to trustee/representative roles only

topics.example: A company holds shares of a parent as an executor of a deceased member's estate and retains voting rights on them.
remember: Subsidiary cannot hold parent shares under Section 19 unless falling in 3 specific exceptions.
No voting rights exist on pre-acquisition shares retained under exception (c).
mistakes: Believing a subsidiary can vote on shares it held before becoming a subsidiary.

quiz.q: Under Section 19, an allotment of shares by a holding company to its subsidiary is:
o: Valid if passed by special resolution
quiz.why: Section 19 specifically states that any such allotment or transfer of shares is void.

quiz.q: A subsidiary holding shares in its holding company can exercise voting rights when holding as:
o: A shareholder prior to becoming a subsidiary
A nominee for the holding company
quiz.why: Voting rights are allowed only for shares held as a legal representative of a deceased member or as a trustee.

topics.title: Objectives, Scope, and Exemptions under AS 21
explain: AS 21 lays down principles for presenting financial information of a group as one entity.
The standard applies to groups under the control of a parent enterprise.
AS 21 does not deal with amalgamations, associates, or joint ventures.
Parent standalone accounts must record subsidiary investments under AS 13.
Exemption from CFS applies to unlisted intermediate subsidiaries with no member objection.
Consolidation rules apply equally to non-corporate entities like LLPs and partnership firms.

flow.title: Checking Exemption from CFS Preparation
steps: Check if company is an intermediate subsidiary
Verify securities are unlisted and not being listed
Intimate all members in writing without receiving objection
Confirm parent files compliant CFS with ROC
If all met, exemption from CFS is granted

topics.example: A private intermediate subsidiary does not prepare CFS because its ultimate parent files compliant CFS with the Registrar.
remember: AS 21 came into effect for periods starting on or after 1-4-2001.
Investments in subsidiaries are accounted under AS 13 in parent standalone statements.
mistakes: Assuming AS 21 covers amalgamations and joint ventures instead of AS 14, AS 23, or AS 27.

quiz.q: In separate financial statements of the parent, investments in subsidiaries are accounted under:
quiz.why: AS 21 explicitly requires separate financial statements to account for subsidiary investments under AS 13.

quiz.q: Which of the following entities controlled by a parent must be consolidated under AS 21?
quiz.why: The term 'enterprise' covers companies as well as non-corporate forms like LLPs and partnership firms.

topics.title: Exclusions from Consolidation and Reporting Date Alignment
explain: Subsidiaries are excluded if control is temporary and acquired for near-future disposal.
Near future ordinarily means not more than twelve months from the acquisition date.
Exclusion also applies under severe long-term restrictions impairing fund transfers.
Excluded subsidiaries are accounted for as investments under AS 13.
Dissimilar business activities is never a valid ground to exclude a subsidiary.
Reporting dates of parent and subsidiary should not differ by more than six months.

flow.title: Evaluating Subsidiary Inclusion or Exclusion
steps: Assess purpose of acquiring subsidiary shares
Check if held exclusively for disposal within 12 months
Check for severe long-term fund transfer restrictions
If either condition is met: exclude and apply AS 13
If neither condition is met: consolidate line-by-line

topics.example: A parent acquires shares solely to sell them within 6 months as stock-in-trade; the subsidiary is excluded from CFS.
remember: 'Near future' is ordinarily up to 12 months from acquisition.
Difference between parent and subsidiary reporting dates cannot exceed 6 months.
mistakes: Excluding a subsidiary simply because its operations differ completely from the parent.

quiz.q: Ordinarily, the term 'near future' for temporary control exclusion means a period of not more than:
quiz.why: AS 21 guidelines define 'near future' ordinarily as not more than 12 months from acquisition.

quiz.q: When reporting dates differ, the gap between parent and subsidiary financial statements must not exceed:
quiz.why: The maximum permissible difference between the reporting dates is six months.

topics.title: Components and Key Advantages of Consolidated Financial Statements
explain: CFS comprises Consolidated Balance Sheet, Statement of Profit and Loss, and Notes.
Consolidated Cash Flow Statement is prepared if the parent presents its own cash flow statement.
Line-by-line addition of parent and subsidiary balances is conducted.
Minority interest is presented within equity, separated from the owners' equity.
Consolidation shows overall financial health, true profitability, and group net worth.
It provides a single source document and enables calculating intrinsic share value.

flow.title: Assembling Consolidated Financial Statements
steps: Take standalone statements of parent and subsidiaries
Combine similar assets and liabilities line-by-line
Eliminate intra-group items and parent investment
Present Minority Interest separately within equity
Publish Consolidated Balance Sheet, P&L, and Cash Flow

topics.example: A parent combines Rs. 5,00,000 PPE with Rs. 3,00,000 subsidiary PPE to present Rs. 8,00,000 total PPE on the CFS balance sheet.
remember: Minority Interest is presented within Equity separately from parent owners' equity.
CFS format follows Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013.
mistakes: Showing Minority Interest under long-term liabilities instead of within equity.

quiz.q: Where is 'Minority Interest' presented in the consolidated balance sheet under Schedule III?
o: Within Equity, separately from owners' equity
quiz.why: Schedule III requires minority interests to be presented within equity separately from the parent's equity.

quiz.q: Consolidated Cash Flow Statement must be prepared only when:
o: The parent company presents its own cash flow statement
Mandated by the company's statutory auditors
Total group revenue exceeds Rs. 100 crores
quiz.why: AS 21 requires a consolidated cash flow statement if the parent presents its own cash flow statement.

topics.title: Calculation of Goodwill and Capital Reserve (Cost of Control)
explain: Goodwill or Capital Reserve is determined at the date of acquisition.
It compares the cost of investment with the parent's share in subsidiary net worth.
Net worth equals equity share capital plus pre-acquisition reserves and profits.
If cost of investment exceeds the parent's share of net worth, it is Goodwill.
If the parent's share of net worth exceeds the cost, it is Capital Reserve.
Pre-acquisition dividend received is deducted from the investment cost before comparison.

flow.title: Determining Cost of Control
steps: Find total net worth of subsidiary at acquisition date
Adjust net worth for asset revaluation profits/losses
Compute parent's percentage share of adjusted net worth
Determine net cost of investment after pre-acquisition dividends
Compare net cost against parent's share of net worth
Recognize Goodwill if cost is higher, or Capital Reserve if lower

topics.example: Cost of investment is Rs. 1,40,000 and parent's share in net worth is Rs. 1,28,000; the excess Rs. 12,000 is Goodwill.
remember: Goodwill = Cost of Investment - Parent's share in subsidiary equity at acquisition date.
Capital Reserve = Parent's share in subsidiary equity at acquisition date - Cost of Investment.
mistakes: Including post-acquisition profits while calculating goodwill or capital reserve.

quiz.q: If the parent's share in net assets is Rs. 96.95 lakhs and the net cost of acquisition is Rs. 63.00 lakhs, what arises?
quiz.why: When share in net assets exceeds cost of acquisition (96.95 - 63.00), a Capital Reserve of Rs. 33.95 lakhs arises.

quiz.q: Pre-acquisition profits of a subsidiary are treated by the parent company as:
o: Revenue profits added to group P&L
Capital profits used to determine Cost of Control
quiz.why: Pre-acquisition profits represent capital profits and are adjusted against the cost of investment to find goodwill/capital reserve.

topics.title: Minority Interest and Treatment of Subsidiary Losses
explain: Minority Interest is the portion of net assets held by outside shareholders.
It includes nominal paid-up capital plus share in both pre- and post-acquisition reserves.
Minority share of post-acquisition profits is adjusted against consolidated net income.
If subsidiary losses exceed minority equity, the excess is absorbed by the majority.
Excess losses are not charged to minority unless they have a binding obligation to pay.
Subsequent profits are fully credited to the majority until past absorbed losses are recovered.

flow.title: Allocating Minority Losses and Recovery
steps: Allocate period losses to minority up to their equity balance
Check if minority losses wipe out their equity to Nil
Charge any excess loss to parent's consolidated P&L
When subsidiary earns profit subsequently, allocate 100% to parent
Continue allocating to parent until previously absorbed losses recover
Restore minority interest once absorbed excess losses are zero

topics.example: Minority has Rs. 21,000 excess loss absorbed by parent; future minority profit of Rs. 15,000 is given to parent to recover part of it.
remember: Minority Interest = Outsider Share Capital + Outsider share in all reserves and profits.
Minority cannot have a debit balance unless a binding obligation exists to make good losses.
mistakes: Showing a negative minority interest balance when outside shareholders have no binding obligation.

quiz.q: When subsidiary losses exceed minority equity and no binding obligation exists on minority, the excess loss is:
o: Shown as a negative balance under Minority Interest
Absorbed entirely by the majority (holding) company
Carried forward in the subsidiary books only
quiz.why: AS 21 states excess losses beyond minority equity must be adjusted against majority interest.

quiz.q: If a subsidiary subsequently earns profits after the parent absorbed its minority losses, profits are allocated to:
o: Majority interest until absorbed losses are recovered
quiz.why: Subsequent profits belong to the parent until all excess losses absorbed previously on behalf of minority are restored.

topics.title: Revaluation of Assets and Liabilities of Subsidiary
explain: Assets may be revalued at the acquisition date for consolidation purposes.
Revaluation does not alter the standalone books of the subsidiary.
Revaluation profit or loss at acquisition is treated as capital profit or loss.
Depreciation on the revalued amount post-acquisition must be adjusted in CFS.
Additional depreciation on upward revaluation reduces post-acquisition revenue profit.
Reversal of excess depreciation on downward revaluation increases post-acquisition revenue profit.

flow.title: Accounting for Asset Revaluation in Consolidation
steps: Determine asset book value at acquisition date
Calculate revaluation profit or loss against agreed fair value
Add revaluation profit to pre-acquisition capital profit
Compute post-acquisition depreciation on revalued figure
Deduct additional depreciation from post-acquisition revenue profit
Present asset at revalued figure less updated depreciation

topics.example: Machinery worth Rs. 1,42,500 is revalued at Rs. 1,80,000; the gain of Rs. 37,500 is capital profit and extra depreciation is charged post-acquisition.
remember: Revaluation profit at acquisition increases capital profits shared by parent and minority.
Extra depreciation post-acquisition reduces revenue profit shared in holding ratio.
mistakes: Recording revaluation adjustments in the standalone books of the subsidiary.

quiz.q: Profit arising on revaluation of fixed assets of a subsidiary as on the acquisition date is treated as:
quiz.why: Any profit or loss on revaluation at the date of acquisition is capital in nature.

quiz.q: Additional depreciation arising due to upward revaluation of an asset on acquisition date is adjusted against:
o: General reserve of holding company only
quiz.why: Post-acquisition additional depreciation is charged to the subsidiary's post-acquisition revenue profit.

topics.title: Treatment of Dividends and Bonus Shares
explain: Dividends paid out of pre-acquisition profits are capital receipts for the parent.
Pre-acquisition dividends received are credited to Investment Account, reducing cost.
If wrongly credited to parent P&L, it must be reversed and credited to Investment.
Dividends declared out of post-acquisition profits are credited to parent Profit & Loss.
Bonus shares issued from pre-acquisition reserves do not change total Cost of Control.
Holding companies pass no journal entry for receiving bonus shares; only share count increases.

flow.title: Categorizing and Accounting for Subsidiary Dividends
steps: Identify dividend declaration by subsidiary
Check whether paid from pre-acquisition or post-acquisition profits
If pre-acquisition: credit Investment Account (reduce cost)
If wrongly credited to P&L: reverse from P&L and credit Investment
If post-acquisition: credit Profit and Loss Account as revenue

topics.example: Parent receives Rs. 12,000 pre-acquisition dividend; it reduces the carrying value of investment in subsidiary by Rs. 12,000.
remember: Pre-acquisition dividend reduces cost of acquisition in Cost of Control computation.
No accounting entry is made by the parent upon receipt of bonus shares.
mistakes: Treating pre-acquisition dividends as income in the consolidated profit and loss account.

quiz.q: How should a parent company account for a dividend received out of pre-acquisition profits?
o: Credit to Profit and Loss Account
quiz.why: Under AS 13, dividends from pre-acquisition profits represent recovery of cost and reduce the Investment account.

quiz.q: What journal entry is passed by a holding company when it receives bonus shares from its subsidiary?
o: Debit Investment A/c and Credit Capital Reserve
Debit Investment A/c and Credit P&L A/c
Debit Bonus A/c and Credit Investment A/c
No entry is made; only number of shares increases
quiz.why: Issue of bonus shares only increases share count without requiring any monetary entry in parent books.

topics.title: Elimination of Intra-Group Transactions and Unrealized Profits
explain: All reciprocal balances like debtor/creditor and bills receivable/payable are eliminated in full.
Inter-company sales, services, interest, and management fees are fully eliminated.
Unrealized profit in ending inventory must be eliminated from group profits and stock.
In downstream sales (parent to subsidiary), entire unrealized profit is deducted from parent profit.
In upstream sales (subsidiary to parent), unrealized profit is shared between parent and minority.
Unrealized intra-group losses are also eliminated unless the asset cost cannot be recovered.

flow.title: Eliminating Unrealized Inventory Profit
steps: Identify intra-group sales included in unsold closing stock
Calculate unrealized profit element embedded in stock
Determine sale direction: Downstream or Upstream
If downstream: deduct 100% profit from parent P&L
If upstream: apportion deduction between parent P&L and minority
Reduce consolidated inventory value by total unrealized profit

topics.example: Parent sells stock at 25% profit on cost to subsidiary; Rs. 20 lacs unsold profit is eliminated from parent P&L and group inventory.
remember: Downstream unrealized profit is adjusted 100% against parent profit.
Upstream unrealized profit is apportioned between parent and minority interest.
Mutual indebtedness is cancelled line-for-line across assets and liabilities.
mistakes: Deducting downstream unrealized profit from minority interest.

quiz.q: In an upstream transaction where goods remain unsold, unrealized profit is eliminated from:
o: Both parent profit and minority interest in shareholding ratio
quiz.why: Since the selling subsidiary earned the profit, it is shared between parent and minority in their holding ratio.

quiz.q: Mutual indebtedness between parent and subsidiary is eliminated in the consolidated balance sheet by:
o: Deducting from trade receivables and trade payables in full
Transferring the amount to Capital Reserve
Deducting the parent's percentage share only
Charging to consolidated profit and loss account
quiz.why: Para 16 of AS 21 requires intragroup balances to be eliminated in full from both sides.

topics.title: Uniform Accounting Policies and Preference Share Capital
explain: Consolidated financial statements must be prepared using uniform accounting policies.
If a group entity follows different policies, its accounts must be restated before consolidation.
If restatement is impracticable, disclose the fact and proportions of items involved.
Subsidiary cumulative preference shares are treated as an external liability for the group.
Cumulative preference dividend must be deducted to arrive at parent's share of profits.
This deduction applies whether or not profits are available or dividend has been declared.

flow.title: Harmonizing Accounting Policies for CFS
steps: Compare accounting policies of parent and subsidiary
Identify differences such as inventory valuation method
Restate subsidiary balances to align with parent policies
Adjust subsidiary reserves and profits for restatements
Proceed with line-by-line consolidation of aligned balances

topics.example: A subsidiary using FIFO inventory is restated to the weighted average method used by its parent, reducing reserves by Rs. 34,000.
remember: Cumulative preference dividend is adjusted regardless of declaration.
Non-cumulative preference dividends are adjusted only when declared/received.
mistakes: Ignoring cumulative preference dividend just because the subsidiary reported a loss or did not declare it.

quiz.q: If a subsidiary has outstanding cumulative preference shares held by outsiders, preference dividend must be adjusted:
o: Only when declared and paid by the subsidiary
Only if the subsidiary makes sufficient profits
Whether or not profits are available or dividends have been declared
Only at the time of final liquidation
quiz.why: Cumulative preference shares represent external obligations; dividends must be adjusted whether declared or not.

quiz.q: When a subsidiary uses an inventory valuation method different from the parent, the group must:
o: Adopt the subsidiary's policy for the entire group
Restate the subsidiary's financial statements using the parent's policy
Exclude the subsidiary from consolidated accounts
Ignore the difference if it is less than 20% of net worth
quiz.why: AS 21 requires restating financial statements using uniform accounting policies before consolidation.
